extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, educators, campus administrators, policymakers, and lawyers interested in U.S. Title IX law and compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of substantive legal standards, regulatory requirements, and institutional duties under U.S. Title IX as described in a Wikipedia article. Covers statutory text, athletics compliance tests, sexual‑harassment rules, investigative standards, institutional duties, enforcement, and related case law and guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory prohibition on sex discrimination (20 U.S.C. §1681)
rubrics_metrics.description: "No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance." (opening text of Title IX / 20 U.S.C. § 1681)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory language is brief and is followed by exceptions and clarifications in statute and regulations. This core prohibition provides the baseline legal standard that federal regulators, courts, and institutions use to assess alleged sex discrimination in education programs that receive federal funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designate a Title IX coordinator
rubrics_metrics.description: Each institution or organization that receives federal funding must designate at least one employee as Title IX coordinator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The coordinator's duty is to oversee that Title IX is not being violated and to answer questions pertaining to Title IX. Everyone must have access to the Title IX coordinator's name, address, and telephone number. This is an institutional procedural requirement used to ensure a point of accountability for compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of coverage — recipients of federal financial assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX applies to any school or other education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1988 extended Title IX coverage to all programs of any educational institution that receives any federal assistance (direct or indirect). Grove City College v. Bell (1984) had initially limited coverage to programs directly receiving federal aid; Congress later broadened coverage. Determining whether an entity 'receives federal financial assistance' is a primary threshold for applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three‑part test for athletics compliance (equality among athletics)
rubrics_metrics.description: To meet athletics requirements, schools must pass at least one of three tests measuring sex equality among athletics the school offers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three tests consist of: (1) provision of athletic opportunities proportional to enrollment (proportional numbers of males and females participating), (2) whether the institution is making an effort to increase participation of the underrepresented sex if there is a history of one sex dominating particular sports, and (3) whether the institution is showing an effort to expand the program to the other sex (accommodating interests and abilities). These tests are used by OCR and courts to evaluate athletic equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity in Athletics Disclosure Act (EADA) reporting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Federally-assisted educational institutions must disclose information on roster sizes for men's and women's athletic teams; budgets for recruiting, scholarships, coaches' salaries, and other expenses, annually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EADA data reporting is a statutory transparency requirement intended to provide data for assessing compliance with athletics equity obligations under Title IX and related policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual harassment and sexual violence constitute sex discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual harassment, sexual assault, and related misconduct are considered forms of sex discrimination under Title IX and therefore are prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions (e.g., Alexander v. Yale) and Department of Education guidance have recognized that harassment and sexual violence can deny equal access to education and trigger Title IX obligations for institutions to investigate and remedy. OCR guidance and Dear Colleague Letters have repeatedly emphasized this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of evidence for Title IX investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidentiary standard used in Title IX investigations has varied: the 2011 Dear Colleague Letter endorsed the 'preponderance of the evidence' standard; later administrations moved toward or required a higher 'clear and convincing' standard; regulations and guidance in 2020 and subsequent administrations changed and reinterpreted these standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because administrations have issued differing guidance, institutions have had shifting obligations depending on the applicable federal rule or regulation; these changes have been the subject of rulemaking, litigation, and further guidance. The standard of proof affects how institutions resolve complaints and the outcome in adjudications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and adequacy of investigations and processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations into harassment should not take many months; institutions should have standard processes and personnel for investigating complaints and must resolve cases in a timely manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Obama‑era Dear Colleague Letter urged prompt and adequate investigations and resolution; OCR has cited lengthy delays or failure to investigate properly as basis for finding violations. Adequate procedures include trained investigators, predictable timelines, and documented processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to take immediate and effective steps to end harassment, prevent recurrence, and remedy effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions have a responsibility to take immediate and effective steps to end sexual harassment and sexual violence and to remedy its effects on victims' access to education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR letters stressed that failure to take such steps can lead to enforcement actions including fines or loss of federal funding. Remedies can include interim measures, changes to policies, and corrective actions to restore equal access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate indifference standard for institutional liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions can be held liable under Title IX where they act with 'deliberate indifference' to known sexual harassment or assault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., courts finding deliberate indifference) has resulted in settlements and monetary awards. A finding that an institution was deliberately indifferent has been used as a basis for private lawsuits and OCR enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of sexual harassment under the May 2020 regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The May 7, 2020 final regulations defined sexual harassment to include 'sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking' as discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those regulations also required institutions to provide attainable reporting options and imposed specific procedural requirements (some of which—such as live hearings—were later changed by subsequent rulemaking or guidance). The 2020 rule was notable for being finalized after formal notice‑and‑comment and for being subject to later administrative and judicial challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to provide reporting options and procedural safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations and guidance have required schools to offer attainable options for anyone to report a sexual harassment case and to follow certain procedural safeguards in investigations and adjudications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2020 regulations emphasized accessible reporting mechanisms, and later rulemaking removed certain procedural requirements (e.g., live hearings). OCR guidance documents have detailed what reporting and procedural elements are expected, but practices have shifted with regulatory changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protections for transgender and gender non‑conforming students
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal guidance (particularly under the Obama administration and the June 16, 2021 OCR Notice of Interpretation) stated that discrimination based on gender identity and sexual orientation is covered by Title IX and that schools must generally treat transgender students consistent with their gender identity in all aspects of school life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This coverage has been the subject of changing agency guidance, executive orders, and litigation: some administrations rescinded prior guidance or proposed stricter biological definitions of sex, and courts have both affirmed and blocked different expansions. The practical obligation for institutions can vary depending on which rules and court decisions are controlling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement mechanisms and remedies (OCR, DOJ, courts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX enforcement occurs through OCR investigations and enforcement actions by the Department of Education (and sometimes DOJ), and through private lawsuits; remedies can include policy changes, monetary damages, settlements, fines, and denial of federal funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable examples include Franklin v. Gwinnett (monetary relief available), OCR investigations leading to required institutional changes, and settlements (e.g., University of Colorado). The threat of funding loss or litigation motivates institutional compliance efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to school policies beyond athletics (dress codes, single‑sex programs, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX has been applied to various school policies beyond athletics, including dress codes and single‑sex classes or activities; courts have found sex‑based dress code requirements unlawful under related constitutional/equal protection principles and Title IX has had implications for single‑sex offerings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Peltier v. Charter Day School held a skirts‑only requirement violated the Equal Protection Clause and that Title IX applies to sex‑based school dress codes; 2006 regulations provided greater flexibility for operation of single‑sex classes at primary/secondary level, illustrating regulatory nuance.
